claim: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) is the most common form of focal, pharmacoresistant epilepsy in adults.
source: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) is the most common form of focal, pharmacoresistant epilepsy in adults and is often associated with hippocampal sclerosis.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established medical knowledge about MTLE.

claim: MTLE is often associated with hippocampal sclerosis.
source: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) is the most common form of focal, pharmacoresistant epilepsy in adults and is often associated with hippocampal sclerosis.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established medical knowledge about MTLE pathology.

claim: Optogenetic and electrical low-frequency stimulation (LFS) at 1 Hz for 1 hr resulted in an almost complete suppression of spontaneous seizures in both hippocampi.
source: We found that stimulation at 1 Hz for 1 hr resulted in an almost complete suppression of spontaneous seizures in both hippocampi.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figures 4 and 8.

claim: The seizure-suppressive action of LFS during daily stimulation remained stable over several weeks.
source: This seizure-suppressive action during daily stimulation remained stable over several weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from repeated electrical stimulation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: LFS for 30 min before a pro-convulsive stimulus successfully prevented seizure generalization.
source: Furthermore, LFS for 30 min before a pro-convulsive stimulus successfully prevented seizure generalization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Acute slice experiments revealed a reduced efficacy of perforant path transmission onto granule cells upon LFS.
source: Finally, acute slice experiments revealed a reduced efficacy of perforant path transmission onto granule cells upon LFS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Hippocampal LFS constitutes a promising approach for seizure control in MTLE.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that hippocampal LFS constitutes a promising approach for seizure control in MTLE.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: MTLE is thought to arise from an initial precipitating insult in early childhood, such as status epilepticus (SE), complex febrile seizures, or head trauma.
source: MTLE is thought to arise from an initial precipitating insult in early childhood, such as status epilepticus (SE), complex febrile seizures, or head trauma (Engel, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Engel, 2001.

claim: The most frequent histopathological hallmark of MTLE is hippocampal sclerosis, which is characterized by neuronal cell loss and gliosis.
source: The most frequent histopathological hallmark of MTLE is hippocampal sclerosis, which is characterized by neuronal cell loss and gliosis (Blümcke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blümcke et al., 2013.

claim: Hippocampal sclerosis is often associated with granule cell dispersion (GCD) and mossy fiber sprouting.
source: In addition, it is often associated with granule cell dispersion (GCD) and mossy fiber sprouting (Thom, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thom, 2014.

claim: MTLE is frequently resistant to pharmacological treatment.
source: MTLE is of particular clinical interest since it is frequently resistant to pharmacological treatment (Engel, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Engel, 2001.

claim: Surgical removal of the seizure focus is an effective therapeutic intervention for many MTLE patients.
source: Hence, surgical removal of the seizure focus is an effective therapeutic intervention for many MTLE patients (Englot and Chang, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Englot and Chang, 2014.

claim: For patients with multiple seizure foci or for those at risk of resection-related impairments, surgical treatment is not an option.
source: However, for patients with multiple seizure foci or for those at risk of resection-related impairments, this treatment is not an option.
evidence: This is a statement based on clinical knowledge about limitations of surgical treatment.

claim: Electrical deep brain stimulation (DBS) often targets either the hippocampus or the anterior thalamic nucleus.
source: One alternative for these patients is electrical deep brain stimulation (DBS) which often targets either the hippocampus or the anterior thalamic nucleus (Li and Cook, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li and Cook, 2018.

claim: DBS at high frequencies (HFS, 130–200 Hz at 1–5 V) is currently in use to alleviate intractable seizures.
source: Complementary to pharmacological treatment, DBS at high frequencies (HFS, 130–200 Hz at 1–5 V) (Laxpati et al., 2014; Li and Cook, 2018), either as an open-loop (Boëx et al., 2011; Tellez-Zenteno et al., 2006; Velasco et al., 2007) or a closed-loop stimulation, especially the Responsive Neuro Stimulation (RNS) System (Bergey et al., 2015; Geller et al., 2017; Nair et al., 2020), is currently in use to alleviate intractable seizures.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: In MTLE with hippocampal sclerosis, the efficacy of HFS is rather variable between patients.
source: In MTLE with hippocampal sclerosis, however, the efficacy of HFS is rather variable between patients (Boëx et al., 2011; Velasco et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boëx et al., 2011 and Velasco et al., 2007.

claim: Neuronal loss and/or altered electrical resistance in sclerotic neural tissue impair the efficacy of HFS since stimulation can only be successful when targeting a sufficiently preserved network.
source: This is in line with the hypothesis that neuronal loss and/or altered electrical resistance in sclerotic neural tissue impair the efficacy of HFS since stimulation can only be successful when targeting a sufficiently preserved network (Cuéllar-Herrera et al., 2004; Velasco et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cuéllar-Herrera et al., 2004 and Velasco et al., 2007.

claim: MTLE patients with hippocampal sclerosis may require specific stimulation parameters to achieve seizure control.
source: MTLE patients with hippocampal sclerosis may therefore require specific stimulation parameters to achieve seizure control.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variability of HFS efficacy in patients with hippocampal sclerosis.

claim: Low-frequency stimulation (LFS) at 5 Hz was effective in MTLE patients in small cohort studies, including those with hippocampal sclerosis.
source: Interestingly, low-frequency stimulation (LFS) at 5 Hz was effective in MTLE patients in small cohort studies, including those with hippocampal sclerosis (Koubeissi et al., 2013; Lim et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koubeissi et al., 2013 and Lim et al., 2016.

claim: LFS would be favorable for clinical implementation due to its low duty cycle, resulting in less electric current injection and longer battery life.
source: From a technical perspective, LFS would be favorable for clinical implementation due to its low duty cycle, resulting in less electric current injection and longer battery life.
evidence: This is a statement based on technical knowledge about electrical stimulation devices.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation offers cell- or pathway-specific modulation of neuronal activity and has been successfully applied to alleviate seizure burden in several rodent MTLE models.
source: Optogenetic stimulation offers cell- or pathway-specific modulation of neuronal activity and has been successfully applied to alleviate seizure burden in several rodent MTLE models (Krook-Magnuson and Soltesz, 2015; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krook-Magnuson and Soltesz, 2015 and Zhao et al., 2015.

claim: Optogenetic approaches targeting the hippocampus were either based on the inhibition of excitatory neurons or on the recruitment of inhibitory interneurons.
source: These optogenetic approaches targeting the hippocampus were either based on the inhibition of excitatory neurons or on the recruitment of inhibitory interneurons (Kim et al., 2020; Kokaia et al., 2013; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2013; Ladas et al., 2015; Ledri et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using optogenetic approaches.

claim: In MTLE models and patients with strong hippocampal sclerosis, pyramidal cells and GABAergic interneurons are strongly diminished and therefore would be difficult to target.
source: In MTLE models and patients with strong hippocampal sclerosis, however, pyramidal cells and GABAergic interneurons are strongly diminished and therefore would be difficult to target (Bouilleret et al., 1999; Maglóczky and Freund, 2005; Marx et al., 2013; Thom, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting cell loss in hippocampal sclerosis.

claim: The intrahippocampal kainate (KA) mouse model replicates the major hallmarks of human MTLE pathology, comprising the emergence of spontaneous recurrent seizures and robust unilateral hippocampal sclerosis.
source: We used the intrahippocampal kainate (KA) mouse model, which replicates the major hallmarks of human MTLE pathology, comprising the emergence of spontaneous recurrent seizures and robust unilateral hippocampal sclerosis (Bouilleret et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bouilleret et al., 1999.

claim: In the intrahippocampal KA mouse model, dentate granule cells (DGCs) with their entorhinal inputs, i.e. the perforant path, and CA2 pyramidal cells are preserved.
source: In this model, dentate granule cells (DGCs) with their entorhinal inputs, i.e. the perforant path (Froriep et al., 2012; Janz et al., 2017a), and CA2 pyramidal cells are preserved (Häussler et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Froriep et al., 2012, Janz et al., 2017a, and Häussler et al., 2016.

claim: Different KA concentrations (10, 15, and 20 mM) were used to achieve different degrees of hippocampal sclerosis and seizure burden.
source: To achieve different degrees of hippocampal sclerosis and seizure burden as observed in human MTLE (Thom, 2014), we modified the established intrahippocampal KA mouse model by injecting three KA concentrations (10, 15, and 20 mM).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design used in the study.

claim: The volume of the dispersed granule cell layer (GCL) was comparable between 20 and 15 mM KA but significantly smaller in the 10 mM KA group.
source: Quantitative analysis of GCD in NeuN-stained sections revealed that the volume of the dispersed granule cell layer (GCL) was comparable between 20 and 15 mM KA but significantly smaller in the 10 mM KA group (Figure 2B, 10 mM: 0.24 ± 0.08 mm3; 15 mM: 1.56 ± 0.16 mm3; 20 mM: 1.52 ± 0.11 mm3, 10 mM vs 15 mM and vs. 20 mM p<0.001; n = 4; 6; 5 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The loss of CA1 pyramidal cells was similar in all KA concentration groups.
source: Conversely, the loss of CA1 pyramidal cells, quantified as the total length of CA1 devoid of pyramidal cells, was similar in all groups (Figure 2C, 10 mM: 37.72 ± 8.84 mm; 15 mM: 49.57 ± 3.27 mm; 20 mM: 42.28 ± 6.44 mm; n = 4; 6; 5 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Glutamic acid decarboxylase 67 (Gad67) mRNA+ interneurons were equally lost in all KA concentration groups.
source: whereas glutamic acid decarboxylase 67 (Gad67) mRNA+ interneurons were equally lost in all groups (Figure 2E, 10 mM: 78.33 ± 3.77% cell loss; 15 mM: 93.35 ± 0.71% cell loss; 20 mM: 85.20 ± 4.35% cell loss; n = 4; 3; 5 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: Animals injected with a higher KA dosage (15 and 20 mM), which showed greater loss of NeuN+ neurons in the hilus, also had a larger volume of the dispersed GCL.
source: Animals injected with a higher KA dosage (15 and 20 mM), which showed greater loss of NeuN+ neurons in the hilus, also had a larger volume of the dispersed GCL (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2H showing a correlation between hilar cell loss and GCD.

claim: Epileptiform activity occurred in both hippocampi of all KA mice.
source: Epileptiform activity occurred in both hippocampi of all KA mice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP recordings shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The idHC of 10 mM KA mice showed a smaller percentage of high-load bursts compared to the 15 or 20 mM KA groups.
source: The idHC of 10 mM KA mice showed a smaller percentage of high-load bursts compared to the 15 or 20 mM KA groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: In the cdHC, the incidence of high-load events was similarly low for the 10 and 20 mM KA groups.
source: In the cdHC, however, the incidence of high-load events was similarly low for the 10 and 20 mM KA groups (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The mean ratio of time spent in high-load bursts and epileptic spike rate were significantly lower in the idHC 10 mM KA group compared to the 15 and 20 mM KA group.
source: The mean ratio of time spent in high-load bursts (mean high-load burst ratio) and epileptic spike rate were significantly lower in the idHC 10 mM KA group compared to the 15 and 20 mM KA group (Figure 3D–G, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 3D-G.

claim: In the idHC the extent of GCD and hilar cell loss was positively correlated with the high-load burst ratio.
source: In the idHC the extent of GCD and hilar cell loss was positively correlated with the high-load burst ratio (Figure 3H, p<0.0001, Pearson's r = 0.84; and Figure 3I, p<0.01, Pearson's r = 0.64; both n = 15 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis presented in Figure 3H,I.

claim: Photostimulation at 1 Hz effectively decreases spontaneous epileptiform activity in the idHC.
source: Photostimulation at 1 Hz effectively decreases spontaneous epileptiform activity in the idHC.
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: oLFS reduces the high-load burst ratio as well as the epileptic spike rate in all animals independently of the KA concentration followed by a return to pre-stimulation levels within 2 hr.
source: Automatic quantification of epileptiform activity shows that oLFS reduces the high-load burst ratio as well as the epileptic spike rate in all animals independently of the KA concentration (10 mM: light gray; 15 mM: dark gray; 20 mM: black) followed by a return to pre-stimulation levels within 2 hr ('post 1' and 'post 2').
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4E,F.

claim: oLFS with 0.5 Hz or 0.2 Hz has a weaker antiepileptic effect during stimulation compared to 1 Hz.
source: oLFS with (H, I) 0.5 Hz or (K, L) 0.2 Hz has a weaker antiepileptic effect during stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4H,I,K,L.

claim: 1 Hz stimulation does not have any effect on epileptiform activity in no-virus controls.
source: 1 Hz stimulation does not have any effect on epileptiform activity in no-virus controls (20 mM KA).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4M-O showing no effect in control animals.

claim: 1 Hz oLFS was significantly more effective than 0.2 Hz in suppressing high-load bursts and epileptic spikes.
source: Comparison of the stimulation frequencies in terms of suppression efficacy using the high-load burst ratio and epileptic spike rate (1-('oLFS'/'pre')*100)(one-way ANOVA; Dunns's multiple comparison test (all KA concentrations pooled), mean ±95% CI; *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of different frequencies presented in Figure 4P,Q.

claim: There was no significant difference between 1 Hz and 0.5 Hz oLFS in suppressing epileptiform activity.
source: whereas we found no significant difference between 1 Hz and 0.5 Hz (Figure 4P,Q; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison presented in Figure 4P,Q.

claim: Local stimulation of DGCs via entorhinal afferents in the idHC evokes population spikes also in the cdHC.
source: Local stimulation of DGCs via entorhinal afferents in the idHC evokes population spikes also in the cdHC.
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Population spikes occur with a latency of 8–12 ms in the cdHC relative to the population spike onsets in the idHC.
source: Population spikes occur with a latency of 8–12 ms (mean ± SEM: 9 ± 0.6 ms) in the cdHC relative to the population spike onsets in the idHC.
evidence: This claim is supported by latency analysis presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E.

claim: Local 10 Hz photostimulation of entorhinal afferents reliably induces generalized seizures in all KA groups.
source: Local 10 Hz photostimulation of entorhinal afferents reliably induces generalized seizures in all KA groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The time needed to induce a generalized seizure (induction time) is longer with increasing KA concentration.
source: The time needed to induce a generalized seizure (induction time) is longer with increasing KA concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5B showing longer induction times for 20 mM KA compared to 10 and 15 mM.

claim: Mice exhibit behavioral symptoms equivalent to RS stage 1–5, independently of the KA concentration.
source: Mice exhibit behavioral symptoms equivalent to RS stage 1–5, independently of the KA concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: 1 Hz oLFS for 30 min before the pro-convulsive stimulus significantly decreases the seizure probability in all animals.
source: 1 Hz oLFS as well as (H, I) eLFS for 30 min before the pro-convulsive stimulus significantly decreases the seizure probability in all animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5D,E.

claim: eLFS for 30 min before the pro-convulsive stimulus significantly decreases the seizure probability in all animals.
source: 1 Hz oLFS as well as (H, I) eLFS for 30 min before the pro-convulsive stimulus significantly decreases the seizure probability in all animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5H,I.

claim: In trials in which seizure generalization is not prevented completely, the ensuing seizure is associated with a milder behavioral phenotype (RS).
source: Trials in which seizure generalization is not prevented completely, the ensuing seizure is associated with a milder behavioral phenotype (RS).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5F,J.

claim: The cellular response to 10 Hz stimulation is reduced after 1 Hz oLFS stimulation in sessions in which seizures have been successfully suppressed.
source: The response is reduced after 1 Hz oLFS stimulation in sessions in which seizures have been successfully suppressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by AUC analysis presented in Figure 5G.

claim: 1 Hz oLFS was started directly after the pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus, ongoing seizures were not interrupted.
source: When 1 Hz oLFS was started directly after the pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus, ongoing seizures were not interrupted (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Pre-conditioning with 1 Hz oLFS for 30 min prior to the pro-convulsive stimulus was highly effective in lowering the probability for seizure generalization.
source: In contrast, pre-conditioning with 1 Hz oLFS for 30 min prior to the pro-convulsive stimulus was highly effective in lowering the probability for seizure generalization (Figure 5D,E, without (w/o) pre-oLFS: 91.42 ± 5.18%; with 1 Hz pre-oLFS: 14.87 ± 8.33%, p<0.001, n = 13 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5D,E.

claim: 0.5 Hz oLFS was also effective in preventing evoked generalized seizures.
source: 0.5 Hz oLFS was also effective in preventing evoked generalized seizures (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C, w/o pre-oLFS: 97.73 ± 2.27%; with 0.5 Hz pre-oLFS: 12.12 ± 8.13%, p<0.05; n = 11 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Thirty minutes of 1 Hz eLFS was as effective as oLFS in reducing the probability of generalized seizures.
source: Thirty minutes of 1 Hz eLFS was as effective as oLFS in reducing the probability of generalized seizures (Figure 5I, w/o pre-eLFS: 93.75 ± 6.25%; with 1 Hz pre-eLFS: 16.67 ± 9.62%) and the associated behavior (Figure 5J, w/o eLFS: RS 2.38 ± 0.40; with 1 Hz eLFS: RS 0.33 ± 0.33, n = 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5I,J.

claim: Photostimulation (1 Hz) evoked stable response waveforms which decreased slightly in amplitude over time in non-epileptic (saline-injected) mice.
source: Photostimulation (1 Hz) evoked stable response waveforms (Figure 6) which decreased slightly in amplitude over time in non-epileptic (saline-injected) mice (Figure 6A1-3, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6A1-3,B.

claim: In chronically epileptic mice, the cellular responses declined strongly and rapidly within the first 10 min during 1 Hz photostimulation.
source: In chronically epileptic mice, the cellular responses declined strongly and rapidly within the first 10 min (Figure 6C1-3, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6C1-3,D.

claim: Lower frequencies (0.5 and 0.2 Hz) altered the cellular response much less than 1 Hz.
source: Lower frequencies (0.5 and 0.2 Hz) altered the cellular response much less (Figure 6E–H) as evident from AUC analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by AUC analysis presented in Figure 6E-H.

claim: Photostimulation of afferent entorhinal fibers robustly induced depolarization of DGCs (5.1 ± 1.0 mV, n = 14 cells).
source: Photostimulation of afferent entorhinal fibers robustly induced depolarization of DGCs (5.1 ± 1.0 mV, n = 14 cells) and was occasionally sufficient to induce action potentials (−70 mV holding potential, n = 4 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data from acute slices.

claim: During oLFS, evoked synaptic responses were strongly depressed (reduction of EPSP amplitude to 28.5 ± 9.9% of the original response, n = 14 cells).
source: During oLFS, evoked synaptic responses were strongly depressed (Figure 7B, reduction of excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) amplitude to 28.5 ± 9.9% of the original response, n = 14 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: In non-sclerotic control slices (saline mice), oLFS for 10 min reduced the discharge probability of DGCs.
source: In non-sclerotic control slices (saline mice), oLFS for 10 min reduced the discharge probability of DGCs (Figure 7C, number of action potentials generated per trial at 100 V stimulation, no-oLFS: 1.8 ± 0.5 vs. after oLFS: 0.24 ± 0.15, p<0.05, n = 11 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-attached recording data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: DGCs were overall more excitable in KA mice compared to control mice.
source: Although DGCs were overall more excitable in KA mice, as reported previously in this model (Janz et al., 2017a), the number of action potentials in response to electrical stimulation was significantly reduced upon 10 min oLFS (Figure 7D, number of action potentials generated per trial at 100 V stimulation, no-oLFS: 3.5 ± 0.6 vs. after oLFS: 2.1 ± 0.5, p<0.05, n = 19 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Janz et al., 2017a and data presented in Figure 7D.

claim: The number of action potentials in response to electrical stimulation was significantly reduced upon 10 min oLFS in KA mice.
source: the number of action potentials in response to electrical stimulation was significantly reduced upon 10 min oLFS (Figure 7D, number of action potentials generated per trial at 100 V stimulation, no-oLFS: 3.5 ± 0.6 vs. after oLFS: 2.1 ± 0.5, p<0.05, n = 19 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-attached recording data presented in Figure 7D.

claim: Intrinsic properties of DGCs in KA mice were not altered by the applied stimulation protocol.
source: In contrast, intrinsic properties of DGCs in KA mice were not altered by the applied stimulation protocol (control: resting membrane potential (Vm) = −73.4 ± 1.1 mV; Cm = 53.5 ± 3.7 pF; Rm = 298.7 ± 27.4 MΩ; Rheobase = 150.8 ± 14.1 pA; n = 27 cells; after oLFS: Vm = −74.8 ± 1.3 mV; Cm = 56.4 ± 7.5 pF; Rm = 313.9 ± 36.8 MΩ; Rheobase = 153.3 ± 26.4 pA; n = 14 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data showing no significant changes in intrinsic properties.

claim: KA-treated mice have strongly reduced inhibition in the sclerotic hippocampus which is most likely due to the loss of inhibitory interneurons.
source: Additionally, we measured spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) of DGCs in slices of control and epileptic mice and confirmed that KA-treated mice have strongly reduced inhibition in the sclerotic hippocampus which is most likely due to the loss of inhibitory interneurons (Figure 7E, sIPSCs frequency: saline 3.9 ± 0.5 Hz vs. KA 0.4 ± 0.2 Hz, p<0.05, n = 5 cells; sIPSCs amplitude: saline 24.0 ± 2.1 pA vs. KA 80.4 ± 15.2 pA, p<0.05, n = 4 cells, all at +20 mV).
evidence: This claim is supported by sIPSC recording data presented in Figure 7E and inference about the cause.

claim: During 2 weeks of daily eLFS, spontaneous epileptiform activity was successfully suppressed in each eLFS session but returned to reference level during the following 2 hr.
source: During these 2 weeks, spontaneous epileptiform activity was successfully suppressed in each eLFS session but returned to reference level during the following 2 hr (Figure 8B–G, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by repeated LFP recording data presented in Figure 8B-G.

claim: Compared to the first reference recording, epileptiform activity remained unchanged in the intermittent reference recordings.
source: Compared to the first reference recording, epileptiform activity remained unchanged in the intermittent reference recordings (Figure 8H, Figure 8—source data 1; Figure 8J).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference LFP data presented in Figure 8H,J.

claim: 3 hr continuous eLFS effectively reduces the high-load burst ratio over the whole stimulation period, reoccurring in a lower manner within 1 hr after stimulation.
source: 3 hr continuous eLFS effectively reduces the high-load burst ratio over the whole stimulation period, reoccurring in a lower manner within 1 hr after stimulation (Two-way ANOVA; Tukey's multiple comparison test ***p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8I.

claim: An initial 30 min eLFS and 10 min 'on-off' stimulation protocol abolishes epileptic spikes during the stimulation cycle.
source: An initial 30 min eLFS and 10 min 'on-off' stimulation protocol abolishes epileptic spikes during the stimulation cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8K,L.

claim: Approximately 40 min after the last 10 min eLFS the epileptic spike rate starts to rise again.
source: Approximately 40 min after the last 10 min eLFS the epileptic spike rate starts to rise again.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8K,L.

claim: Mice with a misplaced stimulation electrode showed no reduction of the high-load burst ratio.
source: Interestingly, mice with a misplaced stimulation electrode (i.e. not in the dentate gyrus, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, n = 3) showed no reduction of the high-load burst ratio (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, pre: 0.16 ± 0.02; eLFS: 0.15 ± 0.03; post 1: 0.15 ± 0.02; post 2: 0.17 ± 0.03; n = 3 animals)
evidence: This claim is supported by control data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mice with a misplaced stimulation electrode showed only a slight reduction of the epileptic spike rate during eLFS.
source: and only a slight reduction of the epileptic spike rate during eLFS (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, pre: 0.59 ± 0.05 Hz; eLFS: 0.43 ± 0.05 Hz; post 1: 0.60 ± 0.06; post 2: 0.71 ± 0.10; pre vs. eLFS p<0.01; n = 3 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by control data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The stimulation target, i.e. the dentate gyrus, is important for a successful seizure interference in the intrahippocampal KA mouse model.
source: This suggests that the stimulation target, i.e. the dentate gyrus, is important for a successful seizure interference in the intrahippocampal KA mouse model (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of correctly and incorrectly placed electrodes.

claim: Different KA concentrations resulted in variable degrees of histopathological changes and the development of spontaneous recurrent epileptiform activity.
source: We found that different KA concentrations resulted in variable degrees of histopathological changes and the development of spontaneous recurrent epileptiform activity as previously described for 20 mM KA injection (Janz et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 2 and 3, and a citation to Janz et al., 2017b.

claim: Cell death of hilar neurons increased with the KA dose, whereas DGCs survived equally but dispersed more strongly.
source: In particular, cell death of hilar neurons increased with the KA dose, whereas DGCs survived equally but dispersed more strongly.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 2.

claim: GCD appeared to be related to the amount of cell loss in the hilus in human patients.
source: This is in line with previous reports from human patients, showing that GCD appeared to be related to the amount of cell loss in the hilus (Houser, 1990) and that DGCs survive in the sclerotic tissue (Thom, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Houser, 1990 and Thom, 2014.

claim: DGCs survive in the sclerotic tissue in human patients.
source: This is in line with previous reports from human patients, showing that GCD appeared to be related to the amount of cell loss in the hilus (Houser, 1990) and that DGCs survive in the sclerotic tissue (Thom, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thom, 2014.

claim: The sclerotic hippocampus in the intrahippocampal KA mouse model is thought to be critically involved in seizure generation.
source: Similar to the human pathology, the sclerotic hippocampus in the intrahippocampal KA mouse model is thought to be critically involved in seizure generation (Krook-Magnuson et al., 2015; Pallud et al., 2011; Walker, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krook-Magnuson et al., 2015, Pallud et al., 2011, and Walker, 2015.

claim: Epileptiform activity generated in the sclerotic focus often spreads to the contralateral hippocampus in MTLE patients.
source: Epileptiform activity generated in the sclerotic focus often spreads to the contralateral hippocampus in MTLE patients (Gloor et al., 1993; Mintzer et al., 2004) and KA-treated mice (Janz et al., 2018; Meier et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in patients and mice.

claim: Epileptiform activity propagated less frequently to the contralateral hippocampus in mice with strong hippocampal sclerosis, than in those with mild sclerosis.
source: We observed that epileptiform activity propagated less frequently to the contralateral hippocampus in mice with strong hippocampal sclerosis, than in those with mild sclerosis, pointing toward a relationship between network preservation and seizure spread.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3 and represents an inference about the relationship between sclerosis severity and seizure spread.

claim: Following KA injection, CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells are extensively lost.
source: Following KA injection, CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells are extensively lost (Bouilleret et al., 1999; Marx et al., 2013), whereas DGCs and their entorhinal afferents are preserved (Janz et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bouilleret et al., 1999 and Marx et al., 2013.

claim: DGCs and their entorhinal afferents are preserved following KA injection.
source: Following KA injection, CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells are extensively lost (Bouilleret et al., 1999; Marx et al., 2013), whereas DGCs and their entorhinal afferents are preserved (Janz et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Janz et al., 2017a.

claim: By positioning the optic fiber above the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus, the study stimulated mainly the perforant path.
source: Accordingly, by positioning the optic fiber as precisely as possible above the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus, we stimulated mainly the perforant path (Janz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Janz et al., 2018 and the experimental design.

claim: CA2 neurons, surviving CA3 pyramidal cells, or temporoammonic fibers were most likely not activated by light delivery.
source: Hence, CA2 neurons, surviving CA3 pyramidal cells, or temporoammonic fibers (in cases of mild hippocampal sclerosis) were most likely not activated by light delivery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positioning of the optic fiber and the restricted light penetration.

claim: 1 Hz oLFS was identified as a highly effective stimulation frequency to suppress spontaneous epileptiform activity in the sclerotic and also in the undamaged, contralateral hippocampus.
source: Using this experimental design, we identified 1 Hz oLFS as a highly effective stimulation frequency to suppress spontaneous epileptiform activity in the sclerotic and also in the undamaged, contralateral hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: LFS at 1 Hz has been used previously to alleviate epileptiform activity in vitro.
source: LFS at 1 Hz has been used previously to alleviate epileptiform activity. In vitro approaches showed that optogenetic activation of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase type II (CaMKII)-positive neurons for 3 min in the entorhinal cortex and electrical stimulation of the ventral hippocampal commissure for 15 min disrupt seizure-like activity induced by 4-Aminopyridine (4-AP) (Shiri et al., 2017; Toprani and Durand, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shiri et al., 2017 and Toprani and Durand, 2013.

claim: Electrical 1 Hz stimulation of Schaffer collaterals in acute hippocampal slices for 10 min diminished epileptiform activity induced by bicuculline.
source: Also, electrical 1 Hz stimulation of Schaffer collaterals in acute hippocampal slices for 10 min diminished epileptiform activity induced by bicuculline (Albensi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Albensi et al., 2004.

claim: Long-term effects of 1 Hz LFS over several hours were reported from in vivo studies using amygdala kindling or pilocarpine rodent models.
source: In addition to this short-term efficacy of 1 Hz LFS, long-term effects over several hours (60 min continuous stimulation or alternating periods of 15 min on/off for 4 hr) were reported from in vivo studies using amygdala kindling or pilocarpine rodent models targeting the ventral hippocampal commissure or entorhinal cortex (Rashid et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rashid et al., 2012 and Xu et al., 2016.

claim: Most optogenetic studies decreased network activity either by direct inhibition of hippocampal principal cells or by activating GABAergic interneurons.
source: Most optogenetic studies decreased network activity either by direct inhibition of hippocampal principal cells or by activating GABAergic interneurons (Kokaia et al., 2013; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2013; Ladas et al., 2015; Ledri et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple optogenetic studies.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of mossy cells in the dorsal dentate gyrus can control electrographic seizures, but the effect was much weaker than with direct inhibition of DGCs.
source: More recently, Bui et al., 2018 showed that optogenetic stimulation of mossy cells in the dorsal dentate gyrus can control electrographic seizures, but the effect was much weaker than with direct inhibition of DGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bui et al., 2018.

claim: Local 1 Hz photostimulation of entorhinal afferents effectively suppressed epileptiform activity in both hippocampi independent of the severity of hippocampal sclerosis.
source: Accordingly, local 1 Hz photostimulation of entorhinal afferents effectively suppressed epileptiform activity in both hippocampi independent of the severity of hippocampal sclerosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Lower stimulation frequencies (0.5 and 0.2 Hz) were less effective than 1 Hz.
source: Lower stimulation frequencies (0.5 and 0.2 Hz) were less effective.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: LFS is not effective in inducing synaptic depression in sclerotic human hippocampal slices.
source: Supporting this notion, LFS is not effective in inducing synaptic depression in sclerotic human hippocampal slices (Beck et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beck et al., 2000.

claim: LFS drives the hippocampal network into a stable state, reducing the probability of seizures while LFS is ongoing.
source: Concerning acute seizure-suppressive effects, we suggest that LFS drives the hippocampal network into a stable state, reducing the probability of seizures while LFS is ongoing.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Evoked interictal-like discharges elicit anti-epileptic effects, contingent on the network state as well as stimulus amplitude and frequency.
source: This hypothesis is supported by Chang et al., 2018 who showed that evoked interictal-like discharges elicit anti-epileptic effects, contingent on the network state as well as stimulus amplitude and frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chang et al., 2018.

claim: oLFS of entorhinal afferents may introduce glutamatergic synaptic perturbation followed by transient suppression of neuronal activity.
source: In line with this interpretation, oLFS of entorhinal afferents may introduce glutamatergic synaptic perturbation followed by transient suppression of neuronal activity (de Curtis et al., 2001; de Curtis and Avanzini, 2001; Muldoon et al., 2015) and thus may interfere with recurrent generation of epileptiform activity (Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Curtis et al., 2001, de Curtis and Avanzini, 2001, Muldoon et al., 2015, and Chang et al., 2018.

claim: LFS improved cognitive function in pilocarpine-injected rats.
source: However, Wang et al., 2020 demonstrated that LFS improved cognitive function in pilocarpine-injected rats.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: 1 Hz LFS in the dentate gyrus is a highly efficient approach to interfere with seizure generation in the MTLE mouse model with hippocampal sclerosis.
source: In conclusion, our study identified 1 Hz LFS in the dentate gyrus as a highly efficient approach to interfere with seizure generation in the MTLE mouse model with hippocampal sclerosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of LFS was largely driven by repetitive activation of DGCs residing in the sclerotic seizure focus.
source: We demonstrated that the effect was largely driven by repetitive activation of DGCs residing in the sclerotic seizure focus, and we have shed light on the associated cellular mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, particularly from the slice experiments.

claim: The findings may pave the way for effective seizure control in one of the most common forms of drug-resistant epilepsy.
source: Considering the potential for clinical translation, our findings may pave the way for effective seizure control in one of the most common forms of drug-resistant epilepsy.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential clinical implications of the findings.

claim: Experiments were conducted with adult (8–12 weeks) transgenic male mice (C57BL/6-Tg(Thy1-eGFP)-M-Line).
source: Experiments were conducted with adult (8–12 weeks) transgenic male mice (C57BL/6-Tg(Thy1-eGFP)-M-Line) (Feng et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: In total, 96 mice were used for this study.
source: In total, 96 mice were used for this study.
evidence: This is a statement about the sample size of the study.

claim: All animal procedures were carried out under the guidelines of the European Community's Council Directive of September 22, 2010 (2010/63/EU) and were approved by the regional council (Regierungspräsidium Freiburg).
source: All animal procedures were carried out under the guidelines of the European Community's Council Directive of September 22, 2010 (2010/63/EU) and were approved by the regional council (Regierungspräsidium Freiburg).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: Mice were injected with KA or saline into the right dorsal hippocampus.
source: Mice were injected with KA or saline into the right dorsal hippocampus (KA: n = 53, saline: n = 5 for in vivo experiments and KA: n = 34, saline: n = 4 for acute slice electrophysiology), as described previously (Heinrich et al., 2006; Häussler et al., 2012; Janz et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure with citations to previous studies.

claim: Mice that did not have SE or died due to KA treatment or surgical procedures were excluded from further experiments.
source: Mice that did not have SE (n = 5) or died due to KA treatment (n = 18) or surgical procedures (n = 2) were excluded from further experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: For optogenetic stimulation of entorhinal fibers, KA- and saline-treated animals were stereotaxically injected with a recombinant adeno-associated virus (AAV) carrying the genomic sequences for ChR2 fused to mCherry under the control of the CaMKIIa promoter into the ipsilateral medial entorhinal cortex.
source: For optogenetic stimulation of entorhinal fibers, KA- and saline-treated animals were stereotaxically injected with a recombinant adeno-associated virus (AAV, 0.45 µl; n = 50 for in vivo experiments and n = 28 for acute slice electrophysiology), carrying the genomic sequences for ChR2 fused to mCherry under the control of the CaMKIIa promoter (AAV1.CaMKIIa.hChR2(H134R)-mCherry.WPRE.hGH; Penn Vector Core, Pennsylvania, USA) into the ipsilateral medial entorhinal cortex in the same surgery (Janz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for viral injection.

claim: For in vivo experiments Teflon-coated platinum-iridium wires were implanted 16 days after injections at three hippocampal positions: ipsilateral dorsal (idHC), ipsilateral ventral (ivHC) and contralateral dorsal (cdHC).
source: For in vivo experiments Teflon-coated platinum-iridium wires (125 µm diameter; World Precision Instruments, Sarasota, Florida, USA) were implanted 16 days after injections at three hippocampal positions as described previously (Janz et al., 2018): ipsilateral dorsal (idHC), ipsilateral ventral (ivHC) and contralateral dorsal (cdHC).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for electrode implantation.

claim: All animals were additionally implanted with an optic fiber in the same position as the idHC electrode, but at a 30° angle.
source: All animals were additionally implanted with an optic fiber (ferrule 1.25 mm, cannula 200 µm diameters; Prizmatix Ltd., Givat-Shmuel, Israel) in the same position as the idHC electrode, but at a 30° angle.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for optic fiber implantation.

claim: For electrical stimulation, 11 animals received an additional electrode (coated with nanostructured platinum), in parallel to the optic fiber.
source: For electrical stimulation, 11 animals received an additional electrode (coated with nanostructured platinum [Boehler et al., 2020]), in parallel to the optic fiber.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for electrical stimulation electrode implantation.

claim: Three mice had to be excluded due to wrong electrode positions.
source: Three mice had to be excluded due to wrong electrode positions (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statement about exclusion criteria based on histological verification.

claim: After recovery from implantations, the freely behaving mice were first recorded on 2 successive days (3 hr each) to determine reference LFPs.
source: After recovery from implantations, the freely behaving mice were first recorded on 2 successive days (3 hr each) to determine reference LFPs (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for baseline recordings.

claim: On days 21–28 after KA and virus injection, photostimulation with pulsed blue light (460 nm; 50 ms pulse duration; 150 mW/mm² at the fiber tip) was applied at low frequencies (1, 0.5, or 0.2 Hz) to test the effect of oLFS on spontaneous epileptiform activity.
source: On days 21–28 after KA and virus injection (10, 15, or 20 mM KA, AAV1.CamKIIa.ChR2-mCherry), photostimulation with pulsed blue light (460 nm; 50 ms pulse duration; 150 mW/mm² at the fiber tip; blue LED, Prizmatix Ltd.) was applied at low frequencies (1, 0.5, or 0.2 Hz) to test the effect of oLFS on spontaneous epileptiform activity.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for optogenetic stimulation.

claim: The radius of light emission with sufficient power to activate ChR2 did not exceed 500 µm.
source: Taking into account the restricted penetration depth of 473 nm light in brain tissue (Yizhar et al., 2011) and an output of 150 mW/mm² at the tip of our optic fiber, we estimated that in our case the radius of light emission with sufficient power to activate ChR2 did not exceed 500 µm (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an estimation based on known properties of light penetration in brain tissue and a citation to Yizhar et al., 2011.

claim: Recording sessions were divided into four sub-sessions: 'pre' - 1 hr before oLFS; 'oLFS' - 1 hr during oLFS; 'post 1' and 'post 2' - first hour and second hour after oLFS.
source: Recording sessions were divided into four sub-sessions: 'pre' - 1 hr before oLFS; 'oLFS' - 1 hr during oLFS; 'post 1' and 'post 2' - first hour and second hour after oLFS (Figure 1A, week 4).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for recording sessions.

claim: For each frequency, 2 trials were performed on different days.
source: For each frequency, we performed 2 trials on different days.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the intrahippocampal mouse model spontaneous epileptiform activity is frequent but rarely generalizes.
source: Since in the intrahippocampal mouse model spontaneous epileptiform activity is frequent but rarely generalizes we evoked behavioral seizures by 10 Hz photostimulation (25 ms pulse duration) and assessed the effect of oLFS before or after the pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus (Figure 1A, week 5).
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of the animal model.

claim: The minimum duration sufficient to trigger a behavioral seizure for each animal was determined by systematically increasing the stimulation duration (in 1 s steps).
source: To determine the minimum duration sufficient to trigger a behavioral seizure for each animal (identification of seizure threshold), we systematically increased the stimulation duration (in 1 s steps).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for determining seizure threshold.

claim: Each evoked seizure was visually inspected on the electrophysiological as well as behavioral level.
source: Each evoked seizure was visually inspected on the electrophysiological as well as behavioral level.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure.

claim: Generic features of evoked seizures were assessed as described by Jirsa et al., 2014 and motor symptoms according to the Racine scale.
source: We assessed generic features as described by Jirsa et al., 2014 and motor symptoms according to the Racine scale (Racine, 1972).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure with citations to established methods.

claim: The identified seizure threshold was validated for robust seizure induction for at least 3 times in each animal.
source: The identified seizure threshold was then validated for robust seizure induction for at least 3 times in each animal.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for validating seizure threshold.

claim: In subsequent 'preconditioning' oLFS sessions, photostimulation at 1 or 0.5 Hz was performed for 30 min before applying the pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus.
source: In subsequent 'preconditioning' oLFS sessions, photostimulation at 1 or 0.5 Hz was performed for 30 min before applying the pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for preconditioning experiments.

claim: For both frequencies, a minimum of 3 trials was performed on different days.
source: For both frequencies, a minimum of 3 trials was performed on different days.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In a subset of mice (n = 5), the efficacy of the pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus was tested again after the preconditioning experiments to exclude confounding effects of habituation.
source: In a subset of mice (n = 5), the efficacy of the pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus was tested again after the preconditioning experiments to exclude confounding effects of habituation.
evidence: This is a description of a control experiment to rule out habituation effects.

claim: Reference LFPs were recorded for 3 hr 19–21 days after injections (15 mM KA, AAV1.CamKIIa.ChR2-mCherry), that is immediately before stimulation experiments, and after weeks 5 and 6.
source: Reference LFPs were recorded for 3 hr (Figure 1B, week 3) 19–21 days after injections (15 mM KA, AAV1.CamKIIa.ChR2-mCherry), that is immediately before stimulation experiments, and after weeks 5 and 6.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for reference recordings in electrical stimulation experiments.

claim: Stimulation experiments consisted of 30 min eLFS followed by optogenetic 10 Hz seizure induction.
source: Stimulation experiments consisted of 30 min eLFS (biphasic rectangular current pulses: 400 μs phase duration, ±200 μA amplitude, anodic first; MC stimulus II software, STG1004, Smart Ephys/Multi-Channel Systems, Reutlingen, Germany) followed by optogenetic 10 Hz seizure induction (seizure threshold was determined as described above, Figure 1B, week 4).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for electrical stimulation experiments.

claim: Mice were electrically stimulated daily for 1 hr (1 Hz) over 2 weeks (2 × 5 days) during LFP recordings following the standard paradigm ('pre', 'eLFS', 'post 1' and 'post 2', 1 hr each).
source: Then, we applied eLFS to interfere with spontaneous epileptiform activity: mice were electrically stimulated daily for 1 hr (1 Hz) over 2 weeks (2 × 5 days) during LFP recordings following our standard paradigm ('pre', 'eLFS', 'post 1' and 'post 2', 1 hr each, Figure 1B, weeks 5–6).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for repeated electrical stimulation.

claim: In week 7, mice were stimulated continuously by eLFS for 3 hr after a 1-hr 'pre' recording on 2 successive days.
source: In week 7, mice were stimulated continuously by eLFS for 3 hr after a 1-hr 'pre' recording on 2 successive days.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for extended stimulation periods.

claim: Mice were stimulated intermittently: initially for 30 min continuously followed by 10 min 'off' and 10 min 'on' phase, which was repeated four times, followed by 1-hr 'post' recording.
source: Finally, we stimulated intermittently: mice were stimulated initially for 30 min continuously followed by 10 min 'off' (no stimulation) and 10 min 'on' (1 Hz stimulation) phase, which was repeated four times, followed by 1-hr 'post' recording (Figure 1B, week 7).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for discontinuous stimulation.

claim: Following the last recording session, mice were anesthetized and transcardially perfused.
source: Following the last recording session, mice were anesthetized (see above) and transcardially perfused [0.9% saline followed by 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (PB, pH 7.4)].
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for tissue preparation.

claim: Brains were post-fixated overnight, immersed in sucrose (25% in PB) overnight at 4°C for cryo-protection, shock-frozen in isopentane at −40°C and stored at −80°C.
source: Following dissection, brains were post-fixated overnight, immersed in sucrose (25% in PB) overnight at 4°C for cryo-protection, shock-frozen in isopentane at −40°C and stored at −80°C.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for tissue preparation.

claim: Brains were sectioned (coronal plane, 50 μm) with a cryostat.
source: Brains were sectioned (coronal plane, 50 μm) with a cryostat (CM3050, Leica, Bensheim, Germany).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for tissue sectioning.

claim: Gad67 mRNA was localized by FISH with digoxigenin (DIG)-labeled cRNA probes generated by in vitro transcription.
source: Gad67 mRNA was localized by FISH with digoxigenin (DIG)-labeled cRNA probes generated by in vitro transcription as described earlier (Kulik et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for FISH with a citation to a previous study.

claim: For immunofluorescence staining, free-floating sections were pre-treated in 10% normal horse serum in phosphate buffer (PB) for 1 hr.
source: For immunofluorescence staining, free-floating sections were pre-treated in 10% normal horse serum (Vectorlabs, Burlingame, California, USA) in phosphate buffer (PB) for 1 hr.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for immunohistochemistry.

claim: Slices were incubated first with guinea-pig anti-NeuN (1:500) overnight at 4°C and then with a donkey anti-guinea-pig Cy5-conjugated antibody for 2.5 hr at RT (1:200).
source: Subsequently, slices were incubated first with guinea-pig anti-NeuN (1:500; Synaptic Systems, Göttingen, Germany) overnight at 4°C and then with a donkey anti-guinea-pig Cy5-conjugated antibody for 2.5 hr at RT (1:200, Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories Inc, West Grove, Pennsylvania, USA) followed by extensive rinsing in PB.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for immunohistochemistry.

claim: Composite images were taken with an AxioImager2 microscope using Plan-APOCHROMAT 5x or 10x objectives.
source: Composite images were taken with an AxioImager2 microscope using Plan-APOCHROMAT 5x or 10x objectives (Zeiss, Göttingen, Germany).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for image acquisition.

claim: To assess the extent of hippocampal sclerosis, the volume of the dispersed granule cell layer (GCL) and cell loss in the hilus and CA1 along the septo-temporal axis of the hippocampus were quantified using Fiji ImageJ software.
source: To assess the extent of hippocampal sclerosis, we quantified the volume of the dispersed granule cell layer (GCL) and cell loss in the hilus and CA1 along the septo-temporal axis of the hippocampus using Fiji ImageJ software (Schindelin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure with a citation to the software used.

claim: Masking was performed since the evaluator was not aware of the respective KA treatment.
source: Here, masking was performed since the evaluator was not aware of the respective KA treatment.
evidence: This is a statement about blinding in the data analysis procedure.

claim: A region-of-interest (ROI) was drawn visually comprising the dispersed parts of the GCL using the ImageJ polygon function in each slice (around 50 slices per animal).
source: In detail, a region-of-interest (ROI) was drawn visually comprising the dispersed parts of the GCL using the ImageJ polygon function in each slice (around 50 slices per animal).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure.

claim: The volume was calculated based on the area measured in each slice.
source: Afterwards, the volume was calculated based on the area measured in each slice (values are given in mm3).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure.

claim: For the quantification of cell loss, the summed length of pyramidal cell-free gaps in the CA1 region was measured in each section using the segmented line function.
source: For the quantification of cell loss, the summed length of pyramidal cell-free gaps in the CA1 region was measured in each section using the segmented line function.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure.

claim: Hilar cell loss was quantified by automated detection of NeuN+ cells and Gad67 mRNA+ interneurons in the hilus of three dorsal sections for each animal.
source: Furthermore, hilar cell loss was quantified by automated detection (Cell Counter plugin) of NeuN+ cells (size parameter: 50-infinity pixel2) and Gad67 mRNA+ interneurons (size parameter: 100-infinity pixel2) in the hilus of three dorsal sections for each animal.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure.

claim: The percentage of cell loss in the sclerotic hippocampus compared to the contralateral, non-sclerotic hippocampus (set to 100%) was calculated.
source: Here, we calculated the percentage of cell loss in the sclerotic hippocampus compared to the contralateral, non-sclerotic hippocampus (set to 100%).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure.

claim: Animals that showed abnormal hippocampal atrophy (i.e. extensive loss of DGCs) were excluded from analyses (n = 5).
source: Animals that showed abnormal hippocampal atrophy (i.e. extensive loss of DGCs) were excluded from analyses (n = 5).
evidence: This is a statement about exclusion criteria for data analysis.

claim: A custom algorithm developed in the intrahippocampal KA mouse model was used to detect and classify epileptiform activity in LFP data from idHC and cdHC.
source: Then, we used a custom algorithm developed in the intrahippocampal KA mouse model (Heining et al., 2019) to detect and classify epileptiform activity in LFP data from idHC and cdHC.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure with a citation to the algorithm development.

claim: The spectrogram per frequency bin was normalized to values between 0 and 1 and local maxima in the normalized (4–40 Hz) frequency band were identified as spikes.
source: The spectrogram per frequency bin was normalized to values between 0 and 1 and local maxima in the normalized (4–40 Hz) frequency band were identified as spikes.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure for spike detection.

claim: Spikes within an inter-spike interval below 2.5 s were assigned to the same burst.
source: Spikes within an inter-spike interval below 2.5 s were assigned to the same burst.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure for burst detection.

claim: Each burst i was represented by a three-dimensional feature vector yi (= [log10 of spike count; log10 of mean inter-spike interval; standard deviation of inter-spike intervals]).
source: Each burst i was represented by a three-dimensional feature vector yi (= [log10 of spike count; log10 of mean inter-spike interval; standard deviation of inter-spike intervals]).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure for feature extraction.

claim: Bursts were classified using a SOM that consists of nodes representing prototypical feature vectors.
source: Burst classification: bursts were classified using a SOM that consists of nodes (visualized as hexagons) representing prototypical feature vectors.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure for burst classification.

claim: Based on the SOM created with the reference dataset, bursts were classified according to their spike load into high-load, medium-load, and low-load bursts categories.
source: Based on the SOM created with the reference dataset, bursts were classified according to their spike load into high-load, medium-load, and low-load bursts categories (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure for burst classification.

claim: The high-load burst ratio was calculated as the fraction of time spent in high-load bursts (sum of the high-load burst durations divided by total recording time).
source: To assess the severity of epileptiform activity within a recording, we calculated the high-load burst ratio as the fraction of time spent in high-load bursts (sum of the high-load burst durations divided by total recording time).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure for quantifying epileptiform activity.

claim: The automatic detection of high-load bursts was confirmed by visual inspection.
source: The automatic detection of high-load bursts was confirmed by visual inspection.
evidence: This is a statement about validation of the automated analysis.

claim: Whole sessions were excluded if the corresponding 'pre' recording had a high-load burst ratio below 0.05.
source: Whole sessions were excluded if the corresponding 'pre' recording had a high-load burst ratio below 0.05.
evidence: This is a statement about exclusion criteria for data analysis.

claim: The area under the curve (AUC) of each evoked response over the 1-hr stimulation period was calculated.
source: Furthermore, we analyzed the AUC of evoked responses (integral of LFP traces in a defined time interval) during photostimulation.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure for quantifying cellular responses.

claim: Only sessions with high stimulation efficacy (within the 95% confidence interval) were selected for AUC analysis.
source: We only selected sessions with high stimulation efficacy (within the 95% confidence interval (CI), compare Figure 4P).
evidence: This is a statement about selection criteria for data analysis.

claim: Transverse acute hippocampal slices (300–350 µm) were obtained and incubated for 1 hr at 34°C in a solution in which choline was replaced by 1 N-Methyl-D-glucamine (NMDG).
source: Transverse acute hippocampal slices (300–350 µm) were obtained and incubated for 1 hr at 34°C in a solution in which choline was replaced by 1 N-Methyl-D-glucamine (NMDG).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for acute slice preparation.

claim: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed in the presence of GABAA and GABAB receptor blockers [10 µM gabazine and 2 µM CGP55845, respectively; 30–34°C].
source: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed as previously described (Elgueta et al., 2015) in the presence of GABAA and GABAB receptor blockers [10 µM gabazine and 2 µM CGP55845, respectively; 30–34°C; Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices, San José, California, USA); 5 kHz low-pass filter; sampling frequency 40 kHz].
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for whole-cell recordings with a citation to a previous study.

claim: When recording IPSCs, the extracellular solution was supplemented with 10 µM CNQX and 100 µM APV to block excitatory postsynaptic currents.
source: When recording IPSCs, the extracellular solution was supplemented with 10 µM CNQX and 100 µM APV to block excitatory postsynaptic currents.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for IPSC recordings.

claim: Extracellular stimulation was performed using a stimulus isolator (Isopulser) with pipettes (~1 MΩ) placed in the middle molecular layer where the ChR2-mCherry was expressed.
source: Extracellular stimulation was performed using a stimulus isolator (Isopulser) with pipettes (~1 MΩ) placed in the middle molecular layer where the ChR2-mCherry was expressed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for extracellular stimulation.

claim: Five pulses (50 Hz, 0.1–0.3 ms, 20–100 V) were evoked and a minimum of 10 trials was used to calculate the overall discharge probability.
source: Five pulses (50 Hz, 0.1–0.3 ms, 20–100 V) were evoked and a minimum of 10 trials was used to calculate the overall discharge probability.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for measuring discharge probability.

claim: Photostimulation was performed for 10 min using full-field blue light pulses (473 nm; 50 ms pulse duration).
source: Photostimulation was performed for 10 min using full-field blue light pulses (473 nm; 50 ms pulse duration; LED p2000, CoolLED, Andover, UK).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for photostimulation in acute slices.

claim: Data were tested for significant differences with Prism 8 software.
source: Data were tested for significant differences with Prism 8 software (GraphPad Software Inc).
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical software used.

claim: Comparisons of two groups were performed with a paired or unpaired Student's t-test.
source: Comparisons of two groups were performed with a paired (comparisons within animals) or unpaired (comparisons between animals) Student's t-test.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: When more than two groups were compared either one-way ANOVA, or two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test was applied.
